name: Folinic acid (leucovorin)
short: Added to co-trimoxazole for Pneumocystis pneumonia in AIDS: more treatment failure and deaths (1 trial). Anaphylactic shock by vein (one adult). Autism review: agitation 11.7%, aggression 9.5%.
text: Children with autism (by mouth where the abstracts say so): in a 12-week placebo-controlled trial of 48 children (mean age 7) given high-dose folinic acid (the abstract does not give the route), adverse effects did not differ significantly between the groups; no serious adverse events were seen in a 19-child placebo-controlled pilot of an oral formulation at a lower dose; no significant adverse effects were seen in an 80-child randomised trial (the abstract does not give the route); and all 10 children aged 4 to 8 in an open-label study took oral folinic acid with no adverse events. A systematic review and meta-analysis that included 21 studies treating people with autism with leucovorin (the abstract does not give ages or route) found that adverse effects were generally mild, the most common being excitement or agitation (11.7%), aggression (9.5%), insomnia (8.5%), increased tantrums (6.2%) and headache (4.9%). A study comparing oral leucovorin calcium with a wait-list in children with autism and folate receptor autoantibodies reports a low incidence of adverse effects without giving figures in the abstract. These studies are small, and a 2026 review notes that the American Academy of Pediatrics currently does not recommend leucovorin for children with autism. Allergy (other uses): a review describes allergic (hypersensitivity) reactions to folic or folinic acid as rare and says that people allergic to folates may cross-react with folate-like drugs, including methotrexate; a case report describes anaphylactic shock in an 80-year-old given folinic acid with chemotherapy for colon cancer (into a vein, a different route and population). A record with no abstract is titled 'Systemic reaction to leucovorin in a child with lymphoblastic lymphoma suggestive of hypersensitivity' (title only). A 2026 patient-level review of 79 patients in 38 publications on folate-related and folinic acid-responsive epilepsies (ages not given) found no adverse event or death attributed to leucovorin by the source authors, but notes that safety reporting was incomplete and that this does not establish the absence of events. Interaction with an antibiotic (people with AIDS, a different population; the abstracts do not give ages or the route): in a double-blind trial in 92 people with AIDS being treated for Pneumocystis pneumonia with the antibiotic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole), those randomised to folinic acid added to the antibiotic, rather than placebo, had more treatment failure (15% versus 0) and more deaths (11% versus 0; P = .06), time to treatment failure was shorter and the probability of death greater, although neutropenia was less common; this concerns folinic acid given together with co-trimoxazole, not folinic acid on its own. A case report describes a patient with AIDS whose co-trimoxazole prevention of this pneumonia failed while taking leucovorin. No child data on this interaction were found in the cited sources. The cited sources give no data on folinic acid taken with risperidone.
